title: The Museum of Small Things
premise: In a quiet corner of a town museum, Ada and Bo discover that overlooked objects can tell surprisingly large stories. With a clever magpie helping them notice details, they build an exhibit—but must solve a real problem: making it impressive without treating borrowed treasures as if they belong to the museum. Different seeds vary which object is borrowed, what its owner needs, and which display materials are available, leading to different respectful solutions.
cast_and_props: Characters: Ada, an observant child who gathers clues; Bo, an inventive child who likes ambitious displays; Pip the magpie, who notices shiny or unusual details and has its own preference for arranging objects; Mara the museum keeper, who knows the collection’s rules and the owners’ concerns. Places and props: museum_gallery, worktable, courtyard, display_case, borrowed_button, old_key, cracked_marble, tin_whistle, label_cards, magnifying_glass, velvet_pad, rope, lamp, owner_letter, signboard, and a returning_box. Use 2–4 characters in any scene, with props as physical carriers and explicit ownership/location state.
kernels_and_interactions: Observation: Ada or Pip inspects an overlooked object or its mark, creating knowledge rather than omniscience. Ambition: Bo wants a striking centerpiece and gains momentum from accumulating Curiosity or Craft. Care and ownership: Mara protects borrowed objects, while Ada can learn and communicate who owns what and what conditions matter. Cooperation and mistaken belief: Bo may initially believe that a dramatic arrangement is automatically respectful; inspection, conversation, or a failed arrangement can revise the plan. Use observe and tell where appropriate, plus custom scenes for arranging, labeling, lending display materials, checking stability, returning an object, and inviting an owner’s choice.
seed_parameters: Use rng from the supplied seed to vary causal conditions: borrowed object type and fragility; whether its owner wants it displayed, handled only with a pad, shown beside a family note, or returned promptly; available display tools such as lamp, magnifying glass, velvet pad, rope, or signboard; whether Pip discovers a hidden mark or Bo notices the case is too crowded; Mara’s initial Care level; and the museum’s space or light limitation. Initialize every entity property and knowledge slot, including object.owner, object.location, object.fragile, object.condition, owner preferences, character memes, locations, tool ownership, and knowledge values. A run must require discovery and respectful agreement, not merely selecting a pretty object. Goal can be an open exhibit with a stable arrangement, accurate label, owner-approved condition, and either the borrowed object safely displayed or returned according to its owner’s request.
candidate_scenes: 1. Ada inspects the overlooked object in the gallery, learning its condition or maker’s mark. 2. Pip notices a thread, scratch, or hidden name on the object from a nearby perch. 3. Bo gathers small museum objects into a dramatic arrangement. 4. Mara explains that one centerpiece is borrowed and shares the owner’s written request. 5. Ada tells Bo what she learned about the object’s owner or fragility. 6. Bo tests the display case and discovers it is crowded, dim, or unstable. 7. Mara lends a velvet pad, lamp, rope, or magnifying glass when its care requirement is met. 8. The children rearrange objects to give the borrowed treasure space without losing the exhibit’s appeal. 9. Pip relocates a shiny object to reveal a better comparison or a hidden label. 10. Ada writes an accurate label naming the object, owner permission, and handling rule. 11. The owner’s preference is checked through a letter, visit, or message; stale assumptions may be corrected. 12. The team chooses to display the borrowed object with its story. 13. The team chooses to return it safely while building the exhibit around another overlooked thing. 14. Mara opens the museum’s small exhibit and records the final arrangement. Scenes should be reusable, with guards based on locations, ownership, discovered knowledge, stability, permission, and available tools.
constraints: Return Python source through the later implementation stages, not prose. Define 8–16 scenes, with about 5–10 selected per execution and at least two reachable endings: respectful display of the borrowed treasure, or safe return with a substitute centerpiece. Avoid magical movement, impossible physics, mind-reading, predetermined routes, previous-scene IDs, and branch-specific paragraph assumptions. Every scene needs a physical carrier, nonempty factual summary, valid actors, declared flat state keys, and effects that obey ownership and safety rules. Deliberate actions require learned knowledge. Rules must prevent displaying an unapproved or unstable borrowed item, mislabeling ownership, or opening the exhibit before a stable arrangement exists. Use labels for important state keys. The prose generator must cover only actual events and make the final image depend on the selected ending.
different_endings: Ending A: After learning the owner permits display, the children use a velvet pad and careful lighting to show the borrowed object beside its owner’s note; the final image is a small, balanced case where the object’s mark catches the lamp. Ending B: The owner wants the object home, so the children return it in the box and make a compelling exhibit from the old key, cracked marble, labels, and Pip’s discovered comparison; the final image is an open case with an empty outlined space honoring what was lent. Optional variation: the owner permits display only if visitors may not touch, producing a roped case and a label explaining the boundary. Seeds should make these outcomes emerge from knowledge, care, available tools, and physical arrangements rather than names or colors.
